items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: And it was like Duke was writing in those days.

ctx.x: Okay, we’ve got the dominant chords coming.

And this would be for C7, and then there would be slots that say ninths. Here would say diminished, augmented, and you’d turn over and you’d have the whole ball of wax. So I thought this was great. So I took the ninth thing and I put it down and I just happened to have it on F7 see? So I played the F7, no I had it on F9, no I had an F7. So I played the F7, and I turned the wheel, and I just accidentally turned it in the direction of the cycle of © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

the fifths. And the next slot was B flat 7. So I struck the B flat 7 and held the thing down. I turned it another notch and hit the E flat 7. Wow. That’s “Sweet Georgia Brown,” you know? And so I wrote my first arrangement, and I turned it over and I did, instead of F7 I did the ninth chords. And I did “Sweet Georgia Brown,” for trumpet, trombone and three saxes. And I used the five way, no double lead you know. And it was like Duke was writing in those days. And I brought that into the guys and they fell on the…
